support.locus: Hittite ritual idiom kiššari=šši dai- 'puts in his hand' (not checked in local corpora)

cognate: *dʰeh₁- 'put' (τίθημι ~ dhā-) + locative of *ǵʰes- 'hand' (ἐν χερσί ~ háste/hástayoḥ); in the anchor pair also *ph₂tḗr (πατρί ~ pitā́)
drift_or_renewal: the child word is renewed (Gk παῖς/κούρη, not in Il. 1.441 itself; Ved. putrá-). Voice differs: Greek is mostly active 'put into another's hands', Vedic mostly middle 'take/hold in one's own hands' (dadhé, dadhidhvé, dádhānaḥ)
shared_syntax: verb *dʰeh₁- + locative (Ved. loc. sg./du. háste/hástayoḥ; Gk ἐν + dat. pl. χερσί, an old locative) naming the hands as the place the object/person is set
context: Il. 1.441: Odysseus puts the returned daughter Chryseis into the hands of her dear father (πατρὶ φίλῳ ἐν χερσὶ τίθει); Il. 6.482 Hector puts his son into his wife's hands. RV 1.38.1: 'when will you hold (us) as a father (holds) a son in his two hands' (pitā́ putráṃ ná hástayoḥ dadhidhvé). Both are child + parent + hands + *dʰeh₁-; the bundle's prose partners (Dem. In Aphob. 2.15 father placing his children's persons into the guardians' hands; Aeschin. 2.28 placing a child into Iphicrates' hands and on his knees) show the entrusting-a-child setting living on in Greek. Caveat: The collocation is frequent in both corpora (Homer about 30 lines with ἐν χερσί/χειρί + τίθημι; RV about 20 stanzas with háste/hástayoḥ + dhā-), so the cognate wording is real. But 'put in the hand' is close to universal and *dʰeh₁- is the default 'put' verb in both languages, so cognacy would be expected even without an inherited phrase. Only the father + child + hands configuration (one RV instance) goes beyond that. The Hittite parallel is from memory.
phrase: *ǵʰésr̥-i dʰeh₁- 'put/hold in the hand(s)', used of a child in a parent's hands

cognate: *dʰwor- 'double door' (θύραι ~ forēs, both plural) + verb from *kleh₂w- 'bar, peg, key' (κληΐω/κλῄω < κλᾱϝίς ~ claudō, cf. clāvis)
drift_or_renewal: none in meaning; the verbs are separate derivatives in each language (Gk denominative from the noun 'bar', Lat. claudō), so this may be parallel formation on an inherited noun pair rather than an inherited verb phrase
shared_syntax: door noun as object or as participle head with the 'bar' verb: θύρας κεκλῃμένης (gen. abs.) ~ clausis foribus (abl. abs.); fores occlusae (predicate participle)
context: In each case the doors of a house are barred shut against someone: Vesp. 198 and 335 the old man locked in; Plaut. Asin. 759 doors shut to all but the lover; Lucr. 4.598 talk heard through closed doors. Homer has the line-opening formula κλήϊσεν/κληῗσαι ... θύρας (5x) and κληῗσαι κληῗδι. Caveat: This is material-culture wording: a door bar is what shuts a door, so pairing the two cognate nouns' derivatives is natural and may have arisen independently. Gk θύρα and Lat. foris both mean the double-leaf door and both stand in the plural, which suits a shared house vocabulary more than a poetic formula.

note: Slab dominated by Thucydides/Andocides/Aristophanes pivots with Cato/Plautus/Lucretius partners matched mainly on common roots (σπονδαί ~ spondeo, θέρος ~ AV harāḥ, etc.); nothing high-confidence. Two low claims. Leads tested and dropped: δάκνω καρδίαν ~ AVP 1.76.11 hṛdaya/daṃṣṭrā (no Vedic 'bite the heart' in RV); σπένδω/σπονδαί ~ spondeo (shared lexeme and legal drift only, no shared wording); AVP 12.12.8 (= RV 1.32.4 áhann áhim) sits in a Thucydides bundle with no Greek counterpart.
